adds.title: Seven transgender prison inmates awarded €5,000 each in damages for 'truly disgusting' treatment (Malta Today)
adds.summary: Malta Today (29 May 2018): the Maltese civil court (Judge Silvio Meli) awarded seven transgender inmates of Corradino prison €5,000 each (€4,000 for breach of rights plus €1,000 for damage to personal dignity) after the prison authorities held them in the male section, where they shared cells with male inmates, were forced to use the men's showers (often forgoing washing) and suffered insults and 'continuous sexual abuse and violence'. The court found the authorities had 'knowingly and repeatedly' placed them in situations of high risk of sexual and psychological violence; the only alternative offered, transfer to the female section, would have cost them the work and study opportunities they needed to pay for hormone therapy, and female inmates and warders were said to be hostile, so they stayed in the male section. The director of prisons was ordered to pay; the Aditus Foundation human-rights NGO represented the seven women.

adds.title: The lived experiences of transgender inmates at Malta's Correctional Service Agency (Oriana Vidal, University of Malta, 2024)
adds.summary: University of Malta master's dissertation (Oriana Vidal, 2024) interviewing four current and former transgender/gender-diverse inmates of Malta's Correctional Service Agency (CSA), a cohort spanning the last 25 years. It records that after Malta's 2013 gender-law reform CSA practice allowed TGD inmates to transfer to the female section, whereas earlier practice had segregated them in a separate dormitory (staff described the rationale as 'the risks of pregnancies'); participants now receive individual cells in the female section but report residual misgendering by officers (masculine birth names), gender-appropriate clothing and healthcare gaps, and conclude that CSA practice, policies and procedures lag Malta's progressive national gender-identity law. It also cites the 2018 newspaper report (Agius, Malta Today) of seven TGD inmates winning a court award after rights breaches including strip searches, showering-privacy issues and being treated as males.

records.note: Malta's documented practice is litigation-shaped rather than statute-based: the landmark 2018 civil case (Judge Silvio Meli) found seven transgender inmates had been held in the male section of Corradino prison with male cellmates and men's showers, exposed to insults, sexual abuse and violence, and awarded each €5,000 damages — the offered alternative, transfer to the female section, was refused because it would have cost them work/study access and hormone-therapy funding (Malta Today, 29 May 2018). After the 2013 gender-legislation era, Correctional Services Agency practice moved toward transferring TGD inmates to the female section (individual cells), having earlier segregated them in a separate dorm; a 2024 University of Malta study of a 25-year inmate cohort still found CSA practice out of sync with national gender-identity law, with healthcare, misgendering and knowledge gaps.

adds.title: NJCM adviseert demissionair Minister voor Rechtsbescherming over plaatsing van transgender gedetineerden (Nederlands Juristen Comité voor de Mensenrechten)
adds.summary: The Netherlands Jurists Committee for Human Rights (NJCM), criminal-law working group, announced (site date 22 Feb 2024) that it had advised the caretaker Minister for Legal Protection on the placement of transgender detainees: no law or regulation currently governs their placement, which NJCM calls worrying and undesirable. The note highlights the group's vulnerable position (international research documents human-rights violations including discrimination and sexual violence), the absence of official figures on the number of transgender detainees in the Netherlands, and the relevance of CPT standards, pointing to the full letter (PDF) to Minister Weerwind (21 Feb 2024).

adds.title: Advies plaatsing transgender gedetineerden — brief aan de Minister voor Rechtsbescherming (NJCM Werkgroep Strafrecht, 21 februari 2024)
adds.summary: NJCM letter to Minister Weerwind (Leiden, 21 Feb 2024) documenting Dutch placement practice for transgender detainees: there is no law, regulation or official policy governing their placement — the Penitentiary Principles Act only separates male and female detainees — and DJI (Prison Service) confirmed placement is based on the gender designation in the BRP (municipal records) together with case-by-case factors (gender-related physical features, the detainee's own preference, offence background, physical/mental health), while DIZ said it was (unpublished) drafting guidelines. Transgender detainees are frequently placed on an 'Extra Care Facility' (EZV) wing, generally to protect them from other detainees, where they sit alongside people with intellectual disabilities and sex offenders. The letter cites documented cases: a trans woman initially held on a regular male wing at arrival then moved to an EZV; a parole-board appeals ruling (21 Mar 2016, 15/4323/GB) on a trans woman first placed in a men's institution before transfer to the women's prison at Nieuwersluis, who reported intimidation, threats, assaults and molestation in the men's prison; and sentencing rulings by the Limburg court (17 Oct 2017, ECLI:NL:RBLIM:2017:10624, trans woman facing placement in a men's prison) and The Hague appeals court (29 Jun 2020, ECLI:NL:GHDHA:2020:1108, trans man in a women's prison) treating a wing not matching the detainee's gender as making imprisonment considerably heavier. NJCM asks the minister to create CPT-aligned rules placing transgender detainees by gender identity.

records.note: The Netherlands has no statutory or official policy rule on where transgender prisoners are housed: placement is based on the BRP gender designation with case-by-case factors, and transgender detainees are frequently placed on extra-care (EZV) wings for protection, mixed with intellectually disabled detainees and sex offenders — practice the NJCM (21 Feb 2024) says fails the CPT norm of placement by gender identity. Documented placement shows trans women initially held on regular male wings and in men's institutions (RSJ appeals ruling 21 Mar 2016), and courts in 2017 (Limburg) and 2020 (The Hague Court of Appeal) explicitly weighed that detention on a wing not matching the detainee's gender makes a custodial sentence considerably heavier. No court ruling mandating gender-identity placement was found; NJCM formally asked the minister to create rules aligned with CPT norms (Feb 2024).

adds.title: Resolução CNJ n. 348 de 13/10/2020 (alterada pela Resolução n. 366/2021) — diretrizes para o tratamento da população LGBTI custodiada ou privada de liberdade (Conselho Nacional de Justiça)
adds.summary: Brazil's National Council of Justice (CNJ) Resolution 348 of 13 Oct 2020, as amended by Resolution 366 of 20 Jan 2021, is the national framework for where LGBTI people who are arrested or imprisoned are housed: a person is recognised as LGBTI for these purposes by self-declaration before a judge, including at a custody hearing (Art. 4º); on arrest, the place of deprivation of liberty is fixed by a judge in a reasoned decision after the person is consulted about their preference (Art. 7º), and the judge must inform them of the available male, female and LGBTI-specific units and ask trans, travesti and intersex people whether they prefer custody in a female, male or specific unit, and within it general population or specific wings/cells (Art. 8º); the declared preference is recorded and a later change of placement is possible, with transfers prioritised in cases of violence or serious threat (Art. 9º). LGBTI-specific living spaces may not be used as disciplinary isolation, and compulsory transfer as punishment is prohibited (Art. 11, VI–VII). The resolution entered into force after publication (120 days, extended to 180 days by Res. 366/2021).

adds.title: Elas também não são mulheres?: Travestis e mulheres transexuais em situação de prisão no Rio de Janeiro (Dilemas — Revista de Estudos de Conflito e Controle Social 17(2), 2024, e60615)
adds.summary: Peer-reviewed census study (Alves-da-Silva & Bonan, Dilemas 17(2), 2024; lead author also of the LGBTI health division of the Rio de Janeiro state penitentiary administration, SEAP-RJ) of travestis and transgender women in prison in Rio de Janeiro state: 138 self-declared travesti/trans-woman inmates were interviewed inside eleven units deemed 'masculine' in the metropolitan region (April–June 2021, via the SEAP's SIPEN database). It documents that in the Rio state system travestis and trans women are housed in units treated as masculine, with some held in so-called 'neutral' or 'security' units, and frames male-unit placement as a double punishment combined with recurring basic-rights violations; it also cites the 2015 Rio de Janeiro state law granting them parity of treatment with cisgender women in women's units (hair length, feminine clothing, accessories and cosmetics) and national norms (2014; 2020) that let them be housed where they choose, including in units denominated masculine.

records.note: Brazil's national normative framework (CNJ Resolution 348/2020, amended by Resolution 366/2021) makes trans-prisoner placement a judicial, gender-identity-based decision: self-declared status, the judge determines the facility in a reasoned decision after asking the person's preference for a female, male or LGBTI-specific unit (and general population vs specific wing), with placement changes and safety transfers available. Documented practice lags the norm: a 2021 census across eleven Rio de Janeiro state units found travestis and trans women still held in units treated as masculine (some in 'neutral'/security units), with male-unit placement described as a double punishment (Dilemas, 2024). No solitary-confinement or administrative-segregation rule specific to trans prisoners was found in national law; LGBTI-specific living spaces are expressly barred from use as disciplinary isolation.
